title: Addiction and Recovery: A Bible Study on the Long Road Back
subtitle: A five-session study on bondage, confession, relapse, and grace, for people in recovery and the families who love them.
summary:
This study is for people who can't stop drinking or using and wish they could, for people in recovery who know how fragile the ground can feel, and for the spouses, parents, children, and friends who love someone caught and have run out of ways to help. It is also for the small groups and church recovery ministries that gather around them. Its five sessions move from the divided will of Romans 7, through hiding and confession, relapse and the long wait, and the father who runs in Luke 15, to the new life Galatians sets before people who have been set free. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it without preparing a lesson; the leader's primer is the one thing to read beforehand. Every question comes with a note for the leader on what it is after, and every session ends in prayer.

This guide is a companion to treatment and to recovery communities, never a substitute for them. It is not a recovery program, and it does not replace a doctor, a licensed counselor, a treatment program, or the people who walk with someone day by day. Stopping alcohol and some other drugs suddenly can be medically dangerous, so anyone who drinks or uses every day should stop with a doctor's help. An overdose is a 911 emergency. The leader's primer says what to do when someone in the room is in danger.

The study takes two common answers seriously. One says addiction is a choice, and the cure is repentance and a better choice; the other says it is a disease of the brain, and the cure is treatment. Each holds part of the truth, and Scripture will not let either have the whole. Paul describes a man who is both responsible and held captive, and who finds his rescue in a person rather than a technique. The study also refuses to let anyone lead it from above. Many who lead or attend a study like this have never had a body that depended on a drink or a pill, but nearly everyone knows the divided will in some smaller form, the promise to stop that did not hold, and that is enough to take away anyone's right to look down on anyone else. The church has failed people caught in addiction with contempt and with silence, and those who lead this study stand inside that failure.
audience: People in recovery, families who love someone caught, church recovery ministries, and small groups

sessions.title: I Do What I Hate
sessions.aim: To give the room an honest name for bondage by reading Romans 7 in its setting, and to hold responsibility and captivity together, taking the moral account and the disease account of addiction at their strongest without mocking either.
sessions.summary:
Almost everyone who has been caught by drinking, drugs, or another compulsion knows the promise made in the morning and the evening that breaks it. The first question of this study is not how to stop, though that question is urgent and its first answers belong with a doctor. It is what to call the thing that keeps happening, because what we call it decides how we treat the person it is happening to. Two answers compete. The first says addiction is a choice and, in the end, a sin, and it is right that Scripture names drunkenness as sin and that recovery asks a person to own what they have done. The second says addiction is a disease, and it is right that repeated use changes the brain's circuits for reward, stress, and self-control, which is why resolutions give way and why treatment matters; its careful defenders add that a person is responsible for seeking treatment, as with any chronic illness. Spoken alone, the first can harden into contempt, and the second can leave a person with nothing to answer for and no one to answer to.

Paul wrote Romans 7 inside an argument about what God's law can and cannot do, not about addiction. But anyone who has thrown the pills away in the morning and gone looking for more by night will know his voice: "For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do" (Romans 7:15). He admits the law is good, and he says he is held captive. He refuses to choose between responsibility and bondage, and then he does what neither account can do for him. He cries out for a rescuer, and he names one.

keyScripture.why: Paul describes a self that wants the good and does what it hates. He agrees that the law condemning him is good, and he says another law is "holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me" (Romans 7:23). Then he cries out for rescue and names his rescuer, holding responsibility and bondage together without letting either cancel the other.

discussion.q: Before tonight, which explanation of addiction did you mostly carry: weakness, sin, sickness, or something else? Where did you learn it, and whose voice do you hear when you think it?
discussion.behind: Surface the defaults before you teach anything. People bring verdicts absorbed from a parent, a pulpit, a meeting, or the news, each with a feeling attached: contempt, fear, or pity. Don't correct anyone yet. Family members often carry a different theory from the person they love, and both are worth hearing. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Romans 7:15-20 aloud, slowly. What in Paul's description sounds familiar to you, and what surprises you about finding it in the Bible?
discussion.behind: Let the recognition land before the explanation. Many assume the Bible speaks only to people who have their lives together, and here is an apostle describing a self at war with itself. Be honest that Paul is arguing about the law, not writing about addiction, though the room will know the shape of the experience. If someone says that sin living in me sounds like an excuse, hold it for the fourth question.

discussion.q: The study takes both the moral account and the disease account at their strongest. What does each get right, and what happens to a person when only one of them is ever spoken?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session, so keep it from becoming a contest over which model wins. Name the good in each: responsibility gives dignity, and the medical account explains why resolve fails and opens the door to treatment. Then name the damage each does alone: contempt that drives people into hiding, and a diagnosis with no call to a new life. Thoughtful defenders of each account reject those misuses too, so aim the criticism at the misuse rather than at the people who hold the view. People in recovery often say the sharpest things here; let them speak first.

discussion.q: Paul writes both that "it is sin living in me that does it" (Romans 7:17) and that "I admit that the law is good" (Romans 7:16). Is he making an excuse? How does he keep responsibility and captivity together?
discussion.behind: Press on the text. Paul is not shrugging. He agrees with the law that condemns him, calls himself wretched, and cries for rescue. Naming sin as a power that holds him is not denying that the deeds are his. Scripture's word for sin already contains slavery (John 8:34), so the choice between sin and sickness was never as clean as the argument often assumes.

discussion.q: Not everyone here knows what it is for a body to depend on a drink or a pill, but nearly everyone knows a promise to stop that didn't hold. Where have you lived a smaller version of Romans 7, and what has it taught you about looking down on anyone?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication without flattening anyone's suffering; a habit with a phone is not a body's dependence on alcohol. But the divided will is common to everyone in the room, and naming it removes the distance between the helpers and the helped. Anyone may pass. You go first, and keep your answer honest and brief.

objections.objection: Addiction is a disease. Calling it sin is cruel, and it is exactly what keeps people from getting help. Nobody tells a cancer patient to repent.
objections.response: Grant what is true, because much of it is. Repeated use does change the brain's circuits for reward, stress, and self-control, which is why promises give way and why medical treatment matters. Churches have used the word sin as a club, and people have stayed hidden, sometimes until it was too late, because they were ashamed to ask for help. Getting medical help is never a failure of faith. Then make the distinction with care. In Romans 7 the word sin names a power that holds a person captive as well as deeds that person does, which is closer to what people in addiction describe than a clean line between choice and illness. The comparison with cancer also leaves something out, as the disease model's careful defenders would agree: recovery asks a person to make real choices every day. And the Christian word holds out what the medical word cannot, forgiveness for the harm as well as help for the bondage.

objections.objection: Calling it a disease is just an excuse. People choose to drink, and they can choose to stop. The Bible calls drunkenness a sin, and the cure is repentance, not a diagnosis.
objections.response: Grant this its strength, too. Scripture lists drunkenness among the acts of the flesh (Galatians 5:21), and responsibility is a form of respect. Then press on what the objection misses. Paul's own account of sin includes captivity: he sees "another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin" (Romans 7:23), and Jesus says that "everyone who sins is a slave to sin" (John 8:34). If sin were simply a choice we could reverse at will, no one would need a rescuer, and Romans 7 would end with a resolution instead of a cry. Repentance is real and necessary, and for someone whose body depends on a substance it may begin with the humble act of calling a doctor.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you have promised yourself, or someone else, that you would stop, and what goes on inside you in the hour before the promise breaks?
sessions.practice: This week, write one honest sentence each day about what you reached for, or wanted to reach for, and when. Don't grade it or explain it away; just name it. If you drink or use every day, let your first honest act be a call to a doctor, or to SAMHSA's National Helpline (its number is on this site's Find Help page, /help), before you try to stop, because stopping alcohol and some other drugs suddenly can be dangerous. If you love someone who is caught, write one honest sentence each day about what you have been carrying for them. At the end of the week, read Romans 7:24 through 8:1 aloud and notice where Paul's cry goes.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, we come as people who know the good and have not done it. Some of us are caught in a bondage we cannot break, and some of us are worn out from loving someone who is. We confess that we have explained ourselves too easily and condemned others too quickly. Forgive the church its contempt and its silence, and forgive us ours. You know how we are made, and you remember that we are dust. Give us honest words for what holds us, and the courage to ask for the help we need, from you and from the doctors, counselors, and friends you send. Who will rescue us from this body of death? We thank God, through you, our Lord. Amen.
reflection: Which explanation of addiction have I lived by, and how has it shaped the way I treat myself or the person I love?
Where do I hear the voice of Romans 7 in my own life, wanting the good and doing what I hate?
What would it mean for me to stop choosing between excuse and contempt, and to say both that I am responsible and that I need rescue?
sessions.teaching:
Begin with something nearly everyone in this room knows, from the inside or from across the kitchen table. The promise is made in the morning, and it is sincere. By evening it has given way, and the person who made it can hardly say how. If you love someone caught in this, you have heard that promise so often you no longer know whether to believe it. So the first question is not how to stop, which is urgent and belongs first with doctors. It is what to call the thing that keeps happening, because what we call it decides how we treat the person it is happening to.

Two answers compete, and both deserve to be heard at their strongest. The first says addiction is, in the end, a choice, and its right name is sin. Scripture supports more of this than its critics allow. Drunkenness is listed among the acts of the flesh (Galatians 5:21), and Proverbs describes a drinker who wakes from a beating he never felt with one question on his mind: "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" (Proverbs 23:35). Responsibility is also a form of respect. To treat a person only as a victim of his chemistry is to deny him the dignity of answering for his own life, and people with long years of recovery often say that nothing changed until they stopped explaining and started owning what they had done.

The second answer says addiction is a disease, and it has real evidence on its side. The National Institute on Drug Abuse describes addiction as a chronic, relapsing disorder involving changes to the brain's circuits for reward, stress, and self-control, changes that can last long after a person stops. For most people the first use was a choice, but repeated use can change the brain in ways that make self-control harder, which is why resolutions fail and why medical treatment is often the first act of honesty rather than a lack of faith. Its careful defenders don't say a person has nothing to answer for; they say, as with any chronic illness, that a person is responsible for getting treatment and staying with it. This account also rescued many people from the contempt of their churches and got them into treatment.

Spoken alone, each answer can do damage. The moral account alone hardens into contempt, and contempt sobers few people up; mostly it teaches them where to hide. The disease account, spoken carelessly, can leave a person with nothing to answer for and no one to answer to, a patient forever and never a sinner forgiven. The philosopher Kent Dunnington has argued that neither model accounts for what people in addiction actually experience, and he reaches back to Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas for an older word, habit, a settled disposition built by choices until it outruns the one who chose. Scripture's way of speaking is older still.

Paul wrote Romans 7 inside a long argument about God's law, which can show us the good but cannot give us the power to do it. Serious readers have long disagreed about whether he describes his life as a believer or life under the law apart from Christ, and this study leaves that open. He is not writing about addiction. But listen to the voice: "For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do" (Romans 7:15). He admits the law is good, and he delights in it, and still he sees "another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me" (Romans 7:23). He does not deny that the deeds are his, and he does not pretend that he is free. Responsibility and captivity sit in the same sentence.

Augustine knew this voice from the inside. In the eighth book of his Confessions he describes how a perverse will gave rise to lust, how lust indulged became habit, and how habit left unresisted became necessity, the links of a chain he had forged himself and could not break, and he reaches for Romans 7 to describe it. He was writing about sexual desire, not drink, but many in this room know the mechanism. He remembers asking God for chastity and adding, not yet. The chain was his own work, and he still could not break it alone.

Here we have to stand inside the diagnosis. Not everyone in this room knows what it is for a body to depend on a drink or a pill, and a habit with a phone is not the same thing. But nearly everyone knows a smaller version, the promise to stop that didn't hold. That doesn't make anyone an expert. It does take away our right to look down on anyone. The church has failed people caught in addiction with contempt from the pulpit and with silence in the pews, and the people who lead this study are not exempt from either failure.

Then notice what Paul does at the end, because neither account can do it for him. He doesn't resolve to try harder, and he doesn't settle into a diagnosis. He cries out: "What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24). His question is who, not how, and his answer is a person: "Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (Romans 7:25). His next sentence describes the divided self once more, and readers disagree about whether that is the Christian's continuing struggle or a summary of the plight Christ answers; either way, the answer to his cry is Christ. And the line that follows is the one this whole study stands on: "Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). You are responsible, and you are held captive, and neither truth cancels the other. The way out begins with a cry for help, to God and very often to a doctor, and the God who hears it does not answer with condemnation.

scriptureStudy.note: "I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do." Paul is not confessing ignorance of right and wrong. He is confessing that knowing the good has not given him the power to do it.

"For I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out" (Romans 7:18). When Paul says it is sin living in him that does it, he is not shifting blame, since he has just agreed that the law condemning him is good (Romans 7:16). He is naming a power that holds him.

"What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?" The question is who, not how, and the answer is a person, Jesus Christ our Lord. His next sentence describes the divided self again, one reason readers disagree about whose struggle the chapter describes.

"Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." The chapter break hides the connection. The cry of Romans 7 is answered with a verdict of no condemnation and a new power, the law of the Spirit of life, which sets free.
"Everyone who sins is a slave to sin." Jesus speaks of sin as slavery and not only as wrongdoing. His promise is freedom only the Son can give: "So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."

"They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it! When can I wake up to search for another drink?" (Proverbs 23:35). The sages of Israel were not naive about how a substance can take over a life.

"For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). The LORD's compassion toward those who fear him is a father's compassion for his children. The God who names sin plainly also knows exactly what we are made of.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long argument behind this session, because the debate between choice and disease is newer in its vocabulary than in its substance. Pelagius, a British-born monk active in Rome in the late fourth and early fifth centuries, taught that Adam's sin had not so damaged human nature that it could not obey God: what God commands, we are able to do. Augustine answered that the will itself is bound and must be freed by grace before it can even want rightly, and the church rejected Pelagius's teaching. Those who say a person caught in addiction can simply choose to stop share something of Pelagius's confidence in the will. Those who say the person is only sick have kept Augustine's sense of bondage and lost his call to repentance and his hope of grace.

Weigh the modern Christian voices that have returned to this ground. Christopher Cook has argued that the divided self in Paul and the divided will in Augustine can inform and extend the scientific account of addiction. Edward Welch, a biblical counselor, reads addiction as a problem of the heart and of worship, in which we serve our own desires in place of the true God. Gerald May, a psychiatrist who worked with chemically dependent patients, saw addiction as attachment at work in every human heart, binding a desire meant for God to things that cannot satisfy it, and he insisted that freedom comes by grace rather than willpower. Each sees something true, none is a substitute for medical care, and together they push past the false choice between a person who is simply bad and a person who is simply sick.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that during this session a man in his sixties, who has never had a drink in his life and says so with some pride, remarks that people who call addiction a disease are making excuses, and that what his own father needed was a backbone. Across the circle sits a woman whose brother died of an overdose last spring. A younger man, a few months sober, stares at the floor.

You will feel the pull to correct the older man in front of everyone, or to let the moment pass. Do neither. Thank him for his honesty, ask the group what is true in what he said, and let someone name it: responsibility matters, and many people in recovery say so first. Then read Romans 7:23 aloud and ask what Paul adds that a backbone cannot supply. Afterward, speak privately with the woman and with the younger man, and with the older man too if you can; he may be carrying a wound from his own father.

Use this to show the room how to hold responsibility and bondage together without humiliating anyone. Ask which voice they have been, the one who scolds or the one who stares at the floor.

memoryVerse.text: What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

sessions.title: Out of Hiding
sessions.aim: To bring shame and secrecy into the light, showing from Genesis 3, Psalm 32, and the letter of James that hiding is the oldest reflex of the guilty and confession the way out, for the person caught and for the family that has kept the secret with them.
sessions.summary:
Addiction lives on secrets: the bottle in the garage, the pills counted twice, the story told at work about a stomach bug. Families learn the same skill from the other side. They call in sick for someone, explain the missed birthday, and tell the children not to mention it at school. This session asks why hiding comes so naturally and why it does so much damage. Scripture's answer begins in a garden. As soon as the first man and woman had done what they were told not to do, they covered themselves and hid, and when God came looking, the man said, "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). God's first question in the Bible, "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9), was not a request for information. It was an invitation to come out.

The session takes seriously the fear that keeps people hidden. Telling the truth can cost a job, a reputation, or a marriage, and churches have not always been safe places to tell it. But Psalm 32 describes what silence costs: "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long" (Psalm 32:3). Then the psalmist stopped hiding his sin and was forgiven. The letter of James asks believers to confess to each other and pray for each other "so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). Confession is never forced and never a public spectacle. It begins with one safe person and one true sentence, and it is how shame loses its grip.

keyScripture.why: The psalmist describes what silence did to his body, "my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long," and what happened when he stopped hiding: "You forgave the guilt of my sin" (Psalm 32:3,5). Secrecy keeps a person sick, and honesty before God opens the way to forgiveness.

discussion.q: What did your family teach you, without ever saying it out loud, about what to do with the things you were ashamed of?
discussion.behind: Start with the inherited rule before anyone's present struggle. Most people learned to hide long before they had anything serious to hide, and many grew up in homes where a parent's drinking was the thing no one mentioned. Let the room notice the pattern without putting parents on trial. Anyone may pass, and you go first.

discussion.q: In Genesis 3 the man and woman cover themselves, hide, and then blame each other and the serpent. Where do you see covering, hiding, and blaming in the way addiction works, both in the person caught and in the people around them?
discussion.behind: Read Genesis 3:7-13 aloud first. Help the room see cover, hide, and blame as the habits of addiction and of the families who live with it: the lies, the secret places, the explanations that always point somewhere else. Keep it descriptive rather than accusing, and make sure family members see their own covering, not only the addicted person's.

discussion.q: God's first question to the hiding man is "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). What does it tell you that God came looking, and that before they left the garden he made garments of skin and clothed them (Genesis 3:21)?
discussion.behind: This is the turn toward grace. God knew where they were, so the question was an invitation. The story ends not with exposure but with God covering them with something better than fig leaves, though the consequences remained and they left the garden. Coming out of hiding is not walking into contempt.

discussion.q: Psalm 32 describes the body's cost of silence, bones brittle and strength drained. What has keeping the secret cost you, or cost your family, that you didn't count at the time?
discussion.behind: Let people name the cost of secrecy concretely: sleep, health, trust, the energy it takes to keep the story straight. Families pay too. If anyone discloses danger, abuse, or thoughts of suicide, do not explore it in the group. Thank them, and speak with them privately as soon as the session ends.

discussion.q: The letter of James tells believers to confess their sins to each other and pray for each other so that they may be healed. Who is one safe person you could tell one true thing, and what makes a person safe?
discussion.behind: Close on the practice, with wisdom. Confession in Scripture is to God and to one another, never a spectacle and never forced. A safe person keeps confidences within the limits that protect people from harm, will not use the truth as a weapon, and points to Christ and to real help. For some, the safest first person is a pastor, a counselor, or a doctor. No one should feel they must confess anything here tonight.

objections.objection: Confession is between me and God. He already knows everything. Why should I have to tell another person anything?
objections.response: Grant what is true. God alone forgives sins, and confession to him is the heart of the matter: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9). No pastor or friend can add to that forgiveness. Then read the letter of James: "confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). The healing in view comes through other people. Dietrich Bonhoeffer warned that confessing only to God can become confessing to ourselves and granting ourselves absolution, and anyone who has promised God in private to stop, again and again, knows what he meant. Telling one trustworthy person breaks a secret's hold in a way private resolutions rarely do. You don't have to tell everyone, only one person who can be trusted with it.

objections.objection: If I tell the truth, I could lose everything: my job, my marriage, my reputation. And churches gossip. Hiding isn't cowardice. It's survival.
objections.response: Take the fear seriously, because it isn't irrational. Telling the truth can have real consequences, and some churches have met a confession with gossip or contempt, which is the church's sin to confess. You don't have to tell everyone, or begin with the people who hold the most power over you. But weigh what hiding costs. Psalm 32 describes a man whose silence was wasting his body, and addiction feeds on secrecy, because what no one knows, no one can help with. Begin with one person whose work requires confidentiality, such as a doctor or counselor, or one who has proven they keep confidences, and ask about the limits of confidentiality before you start. "He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy" (Proverbs 28:13). The mercy may come slowly.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you have never told anyone that you would be relieved to tell one safe person, even if you are not ready to say it here?
sessions.practice: This week, tell one safe person one true thing you have kept hidden: a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a friend who has proven they keep confidences. One true sentence is enough to begin. If you love someone who is caught, the practice is yours too. Name one secret you have been keeping for them, a lie told to an employer or an excuse made to the children, and decide with someone wise whether to stop keeping it. If keeping their secret is what keeps you safe from violence, don't confront anyone; call the National Domestic Violence Hotline first (its number is on this site's Find Help page, /help). Read Psalm 32 aloud at the start of each day.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you came looking for us in the garden when we had hidden ourselves, and you asked where we were because you wanted us back. We have covered and hidden and blamed, and some of us have kept other people's secrets so long we have forgotten what honesty sounds like. Forgive us. Forgive the church for every time it made confession dangerous. Give each of us one safe person and the courage to tell one true thing. Clothe us as you clothed our first parents, with something better than the fig leaves we keep sewing. Make this a room where no one has to hide. Through Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Amen.
reflection: What have I been hiding, and what has the hiding cost me that I have not counted?
Where have I covered, hidden, or blamed, and who first taught me to do it?
Who is one safe person I could tell one true thing, and what keeps me from doing it?
sessions.teaching:
Addiction lives on secrets, and so does the family around it. The person caught learns to hide the bottle, count the pills, and invent the stomach bug. The people who love them learn the same craft from the other side: the call to the employer, the excuse at the family dinner, the instruction to the children not to say anything at school. Over time a whole household can be organized around a secret everyone keeps and no one names. So this session asks why hiding comes so naturally to us, and why it does so much damage.

Scripture's answer begins in the garden. When the first man and woman had eaten what they were told not to eat, "the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves" (Genesis 3:7). They heard God walking in the garden, and they hid among the trees. When God called, the man said, "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). Within a few verses the man is blaming the woman, and the woman is blaming the serpent. Cover, hide, and blame: those three moves are as old as sin, and anyone who has lived with addiction knows them by heart.

But notice what God does. He comes looking. His first question in the whole Bible is "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9), and since the one asking already knows the answer, it is an invitation to come out. The story does not end with exposure. It ends with a mercy we often skip: "And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them" (Genesis 3:21). The consequences were real, and they left the garden. But God covered what they could not cover themselves, with something better than fig leaves.

The fear that keeps people hidden deserves respect. Telling the truth can cost a job, a license, a marriage, or a reputation, and churches have sometimes met a confession with gossip or contempt, a sin the church must confess before it asks anyone else to. Privacy has its place, too, and this study asks no one to confess anything in this room. But there is a difference between privacy, which protects what is good, and secrecy, which protects what is killing us.

Psalm 32, which bears David's name in its heading, describes what secrecy does to a body: "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long. For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat" (Psalm 32:3-4). People who have lived inside a secret know that exhaustion, the energy it takes to keep the story straight and the low, constant dread of being found out. Then the turn: "Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity" (Psalm 32:5), and the next words are forgiveness. The psalm opens with "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered" (Psalm 32:1). The covering no fig leaf could provide was given when he stopped hiding.

The New Testament carries the pattern into the life of the church. The letter of James, in a passage about prayer for the sick, tells believers to "confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16), a mutual confession among people who pray for one another, not a performance before an audience. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing on Christian community in 1938, warned that confessing only to God can quietly become confessing to ourselves and granting ourselves absolution, and that sin wants to keep a person to itself; telling a brother or sister, he argued, breaks through that isolation. The psychiatrist Anna Lembke has reached a related conclusion in the clinic: shame met with exile drives people deeper into their addiction, while shame met by a community that offers accountability and support can draw them back. She has seen the symptom truly. Scripture adds what medicine cannot: the guilt is real, and it can be forgiven, not only managed.

Families need this session as much as anyone. A family's secret is usually kept out of love, but a secret kept for an addiction tends to protect the addiction more than the person, and children notice what no one names. For a family, coming out of hiding can begin with one honest conversation with a pastor or counselor, and it never requires confronting someone who is dangerous; if someone at home is violent or threatening, the place to start is the National Domestic Violence Hotline, or 911 in an emergency. The church must look at itself here, too. A church where no one can say I relapsed, or my son is using, is a church where people stay hidden until it is too late. Most of us have helped build that room.

Confession is not the price God charges for forgiveness. Jesus has already "endured the cross, scorning its shame," as the letter to the Hebrews says (Hebrews 12:2). Confession is how we stop hiding from a God who has already come looking, and it is how the covering God gives replaces the coverings we keep sewing.

scriptureStudy.note: "So they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves" (Genesis 3:7), and then they hid among the trees. The first effects of sin in the story are covering and hiding, the oldest habits of addiction.
"Where are you?" God asks a question he knows the answer to, which makes it an invitation. The man's reply names the engine of all hiding: "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself."

"The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it" (Genesis 3:12). Blame is the third move, and addiction is fluent in it: the stress, the spouse, the boss, the past. Honesty begins when the explanations stop pointing somewhere else.
"And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them." The consequences remain, and they leave the garden, but the God they hid from clothes them before they go.

"When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long" (Psalm 32:3). Secrecy costs the body. The psalm begins, "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered" (Psalm 32:1), and that covering comes when the psalmist stops covering himself.

"Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). The setting is prayer for the sick. Confession here is mutual and joined to prayer and healing, not a public spectacle.

"But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another" (1 John 1:7). Walking in the light is not perfection, since the next verse says that anyone who claims to have no sin is self-deceived. Light means honesty, and its promise is fellowship and cleansing.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long history of confession, because the church has practiced it in more than one form. Some traditions keep private confession to a priest. Many Protestant churches pray a corporate confession in worship and commend confession to a pastor or trusted friend without requiring it. Almost every tradition has known the simple practice the letter of James describes, two believers telling each other the truth and praying together. A group may hold these differences without contempt. What they share is the conviction that hidden sin is dangerous and that God has given his people to each other as a means of grace.

Set that beside the modern instinct that what I do is my own business, and beside the recovery groups that have long made honest speech in company the center of their life together. Read Bonhoeffer's Life Together, published in 1939, on why confession breaks through the isolation sin produces, and weigh it against Anna Lembke's account of what she calls prosocial shame. The secular account sees that isolation feeds addiction. It cannot say who forgives. A serious group should also face its own failures, the gossip that made confession dangerous and the performance of being fine on Sunday mornings, and build a community where the first word after a confession is mercy.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group mentions, almost in passing, that she has called her husband's employer three times this year to say he had the flu, because the family needs his paycheck. She says it as a joke, but no one laughs.

You will want to tell her to stop lying for him. Don't, at least not in front of the group. Ask what Psalm 32 says about what keeping a secret costs, and let her and the room answer. Afterward, privately, ask whether she is safe at home. If she is, help her think about one person she could tell, a pastor or a counselor, and what it would mean to stop carrying this lie with help and a plan, since the family's income is a real concern. If she is not safe, her first call is to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, not a conversation with her husband.

Use this to show the room that families hide too, out of love and fear, and that coming out of hiding has to be done wisely and safely. Ask what secrets they have kept for someone else, and what those secrets were protecting.

memoryVerse.text: Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.

sessions.title: The Pit and the Waiting
sessions.aim: To meet relapse and the slowness of recovery with the patience of Psalm 40 and Lamentations 3, so that a fall becomes a reason to call for help at once rather than a verdict of failure, without ever pretending a relapse is small or safe.
sessions.summary:
Recovery is rarely a straight line, and almost everyone who has walked it, or loved someone through it, knows the despair of starting over. This session asks what to make of the falls and how to live through the waiting, and it refuses two answers. The first says a relapse proves the repentance was fake, and it is right that a relapse is serious, that it involves choices, and that sorrow without change is not repentance. The second says relapse is just part of recovery, and it is right that shame after a slip often drives people deeper and that many stumble before they stand. Each, alone, does harm. The first leaves people too ashamed to come back. The second forgets that a relapse can kill, because after time away tolerance drops, and returning to the old amount of an opioid can be fatal.

Psalm 40 opens with a man lifted out of the pit after a long wait, his feet set on a rock and a new song in his mouth. Later in the same psalm his sins have overtaken him, and he is crying, "hurry, O LORD, to help me" (Psalm 40:13). The poet of Lamentations sits in the ruins of Jerusalem and still says, "It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD" (Lamentations 3:26). Peter vowed to follow Jesus to prison and to death and denied him that same night, and Jesus had already prayed for his return. God's patience is not permission. It is the reason to get up, tell the truth, and call for help today.

keyScripture.why: "I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry" (Psalm 40:1). The psalm names the long wait, the pit, and the rescue, and later the same singer is overtaken by his sins and cries for help again (Psalm 40:12-13), which makes it an honest song for anyone who has fallen after being lifted.

discussion.q: When you have fallen back into something you had promised to stop, or watched someone you love do it, what did you tell yourself the fall meant?
discussion.behind: Surface the verdicts people pronounce on a relapse: I'm hopeless, she never meant it, God is done with me, it doesn't matter. Don't correct anyone yet. Many have heard a harsh verdict from someone else and repeated it to themselves, and families carry their own version: we're fools to hope again. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 40:1-3 and then 40:11-13. What does it mean to you that the same psalm that sings of being lifted from the pit later cries out for help again?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. The psalm does not end where it starts. The deliverance was real, and trouble came again, including the singer's own sins. Scripture's songs of rescue are honest about the next crisis, and a fall after being lifted does not mean the lifting was fake.

discussion.q: The study takes seriously both the person who says a relapse proves insincerity and the person who says relapse is just part of recovery. What is true in each, and what is dangerous in each?
discussion.behind: Hold both. A relapse is serious and involves choices, and treating it lightly can be deadly, because after time away tolerance falls and the old amount of an opioid can kill. But shame after a slip often drives people deeper, and medicine treats relapse as a sign that treatment needs to be resumed or changed. Make sure the room leaves knowing that a relapse is a reason to call for help today.

discussion.q: Peter promised to go with Jesus to prison and to death, and denied him that night. Jesus had already told him, "when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32). What does it tell you that Jesus planned Peter's return before his fall?
discussion.behind: Let the room feel the grace of a restoration prepared in advance. Jesus did not excuse the denial, and Peter wept bitterly, but the failure was not the end of his usefulness. Families may need to hear this about the person they love, and people in recovery about themselves. Don't let it become permission. Peter turned back.

discussion.q: Lamentations says, "It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD" (Lamentations 3:26). If you are waiting, for your own freedom or someone else's, what would it look like to wait with hope rather than with despair or with an attempt to control?
discussion.behind: Close on the waiting, with self-implication. Waiting is not passivity; it includes treatment, honesty, boundaries, and prayer. For families it often means letting go of the illusion of control without letting go of love. Invite each person, you first, to name what they are waiting for, and do not resolve it.

objections.objection: If he really meant it, he wouldn't have gone back. A relapse proves the repentance was fake, and I'm done being lied to.
objections.response: Honor the hurt first, because people who say this have usually been lied to many times, and their weariness is earned. A relapse is serious and involves choices, and sorrow that changes nothing is not repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). A family is right to hold its boundaries after a relapse. But a fall does not prove the earlier repentance was fake. Peter's wasn't, and he denied Jesus within hours of promising to die for him. Medicine says something similar: it treats relapse as a reason to resume or change treatment, not as proof that treatment failed. The question after a relapse is not whether he meant it before. It is whether he will tell the truth and get help now. You can keep your boundaries and still leave that door open.

objections.objection: Relapse is just part of recovery. Everybody slips. Making a big deal of it only adds shame, and shame is what makes people use.
objections.response: Grant what is true. Shame after a slip often drives people deeper into using, and many who now have years of recovery fell more than once before they stood. A relapse is not the end of hope, and the church should never treat it as unforgivable. But a relapse is not nothing either. With opioids especially, the danger after time away is greater than before, because tolerance drops and the old amount can cause a fatal overdose. A relapse also lands on other people: the spouse who believed again, the children who were promised. Treat it the way the psalmist treated his trouble: "hurry, O LORD, to help me" (Psalm 40:13). Tell someone today, call the doctor or counselor, and if anyone may have overdosed, call 911.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the thing you fear most happened this week, a relapse, yours or someone else's, who would you call first, and have you told them that?
sessions.practice: This week, put a plan for the hardest hour on paper before you need it. Name the time, the place, or the feeling when the pull is strongest, and write down one person you will call and one thing you will do instead. Tell that person they are on your list. If you love someone in recovery, write your own plan for what you will do if they use again: whom you will call, what boundary you will keep, and how you will care for yourself and any children. Everyone should know that an overdose is a 911 emergency. Read Lamentations 3:19-26 each morning, and say verse 23 aloud.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you lifted the psalmist out of the pit, and when his sins overtook him, he cried to you again. You prayed for Peter before he fell. Some of us are in the pit tonight. Some of us are waiting for someone we love to climb out, and we are tired of hoping. Keep us from the despair that says it is over and from the carelessness that says it doesn't matter. When we fall, make us quick to tell the truth and quick to ask for help. Teach us to wait for you quietly, and to keep doing the next faithful thing while we wait. Your mercies are new every morning. Give us tomorrow's. Amen.
reflection: What verdict have I pronounced over my own falls, or over someone else's, and does it sound like Psalm 40 or like something else?
What would it look like for me to treat the next fall as a reason to call for help instead of a reason to hide?
What am I waiting for, and am I waiting with hope, with despair, or with an attempt to control what I cannot?
sessions.teaching:
Recovery is rarely a straight line, and almost everyone who has walked it, or loved someone through it, knows the despair of starting over: thirty days and then a night that undid them, a third stay in treatment, a vow made with tears and broken within the week. Families know their own version, the phone call that comes after you had finally let yourself hope. This session asks what to make of the falls and how to live through the waiting, and the honest answer runs between two errors that both sound like wisdom.

The first error says that a relapse proves the repentance was never real. Take it seriously, because it is usually spoken by someone who has been lied to many times. It is right that a relapse is serious and involves choices, and right that Scripture distinguishes sorrow that changes a person from sorrow that only hurts: "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). A family may need to protect itself after a relapse. What this view gets wrong is the verdict. A fall after a sincere turn does not prove the turn was false. Peter told Jesus, "I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death" (Luke 22:33), and he meant it, and he denied him before the rooster crowed.

The second error says relapse is just part of recovery, nothing to make a fuss about. It has truth in it, too. Shame after a slip often drives a person deeper into using, and many people with long years of recovery fell more than once before they stood. The National Institute on Drug Abuse compares relapse to the return of symptoms in other chronic illnesses, such as high blood pressure or asthma, a sign that treatment needs to be resumed or changed rather than proof that it failed. But part of recovery can quietly become permission, and it hides a danger: after a stretch of not using, tolerance drops, and returning to the amount of an opioid a person once used can cause a fatal overdose. A relapse can be a medical emergency, and it lands on other people too.

Psalm 40 holds both truths. It opens with rescue after a long wait: "I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm" (Psalm 40:1-2). If the psalm ended there, it would be a testimony with a clean ending, and it doesn't end there. A few verses later the same singer says, "my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see" (Psalm 40:12), and he cries, "Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me; hurry, O LORD, to help me" (Psalm 40:13). The psalm closes with a plea: "O my God, do not delay" (Psalm 40:17). The rescue was real, and so was the next trouble. Overtaken, the singer neither hides nor quits. He cries out again, and this time he asks God to hurry.

Lamentations was written in the ruins of Jerusalem after the city fell in 587 or 586 BC. In the middle of the third poem the poet says, "Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall" (Lamentations 3:19), and then, with nothing yet rebuilt: "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" (Lamentations 3:21-23). He goes on: "It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD" (Lamentations 3:26). This kind of waiting refuses to despair while the ruin is still in plain view. For a person in recovery it may look like keeping the next appointment and making the next honest phone call, one morning's mercy at a time. For a family it may mean letting go of the illusion of control without letting go of love.

Peter's story bends the same way. On the night he swore his loyalty, Jesus told him, "I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32). Jesus planned the return before the fall, and after the resurrection he asked Peter three times whether he loved him and three times gave him work to do (John 21:15-17). Augustine, writing his Confessions more than a decade after his conversion in a Milan garden, gave much of its tenth book to the temptations that still beset him. The converted are not finished. Eugene Peterson, in the title of his book on the Songs of Ascents, called discipleship a long obedience in the same direction, and that is the shape of recovery too: measured in years rather than weeks, with falls that are taken seriously and are not allowed the last word.

So the verdict on a relapse is neither of the ones we are tempted to pronounce. It is not the end, and it is not nothing. It is the moment to do what the psalmist did: stop hiding and cry out for help, to God, to the people walking with you, and, if there is any chance of an overdose, to 911. The psalm ends with that second cry still waiting for an answer, and the psalmist prays it anyway, because he has been lifted once and knows whom he is asking.

scriptureStudy.note: "He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm" (Psalm 40:2). The rescue follows a long wait, and it is God's work. The new song is meant to be overheard: "Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD" (Psalm 40:3).

"My sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see" (Psalm 40:12). The same singer who was lifted is overtaken again, and he doesn't pretend otherwise. His response is the right one: "hurry, O LORD, to help me" (Psalm 40:13).

"But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay." The psalm ends with a plea rather than a victory lap. Honest recovery often sounds like this.

"They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" (Lamentations 3:23). Written in the ruins after Jerusalem fell, this hope does not wait for the rubble to be cleared. It counts mercy one morning at a time, which is how recovery is lived.

"Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light" (Micah 7:8). The voice is Zion's, the city personified, and the next verse admits, "I have sinned against Him" (Micah 7:9). This is hope from a people who know their fall was their own doing and still expect God to bring them into the light.

"And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32). Jesus prays for Peter before the denial and speaks of his return before he falls. The failure is foreseen and grieved, and it is not final.

"Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death." Paul is writing about the grief an earlier letter of his had caused the Corinthians, a grief that led them to repent (2 Corinthians 7:8-9). After a relapse, the question is not how bad you feel but which way the sorrow is turning you.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up an argument the church had long before anyone used the word relapse. In the third century, after a wave of persecution in which many Christians had denied the faith under threat, the church had to decide whether those who had fallen could be restored. Around 251 a rigorist party in Rome, led by a presbyter named Novatian, held that the church could not restore them to its communion. Their concern deserves a fair hearing, because denying Christ is not a small thing, and they feared a church that made it cheap. The larger church chose a way of repentance and restoration, refusing both to pretend the denial had not happened and to shut the door forever. The argument keeps coming back. Some Christians, wounded by cheap grace, want to make the door narrow. Others, wounded by harshness, want to remove the threshold altogether.

Weigh medicine's language alongside the church's. When the National Institute on Drug Abuse treats relapse as a reason to resume or change treatment, it stands nearer the church that restored the fallen than the rigorists who would not, though medicine has no word for forgiveness. A serious group should ask how a church can keep the door of restoration open without making relapse casual, how it can hold a boundary and a welcome at the same time, and what it would look like to measure faithfulness in years rather than in days, with the patience of a God whose mercies are new every morning.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group, about three months sober, comes to a session quiet and gray, and at the break he tells you he drank on Saturday. He hasn't told his wife or his counselor, and he almost didn't come tonight.

You will want either to reassure him that it doesn't matter or to tell him he knows better. Do neither. Thank him for telling you, because that was the hardest thing he did all week. Ask whether he is safe right now and whether he has used anything else. Encourage him to call his counselor or doctor within the day and to tell one person at home, and offer to sit with him while he makes the call. Read Psalm 40:13 with him. Then let him decide whether to say anything to the group.

Use this to show the room what it looks like to treat a relapse as a reason to call for help, neither a catastrophe nor a shrug. Ask whom they would want to call if they fell, and whether that person knows it.

memoryVerse.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm.

sessions.title: The Father Running
sessions.aim: To see in Luke 15 a grace that runs to a son still far off, before his speech is finished and without waiting for him to hit bottom, and to help families love without enabling: keeping boundaries without abandoning anyone, putting safety first, and caring for the children.
sessions.summary:
Jesus told the story of a father and his two sons to people who were grumbling that he "welcomes sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). A younger son demands his share of the estate, leaves for a distant country, and spends everything. When famine comes, he is feeding pigs and envying their food. He comes to his senses and rehearses a speech asking to be taken back as a hired servant. Then the story turns on one verse: "But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father doesn't wait for the son to reach the house, finish his speech, or prove himself. He answers the confession with a robe, a ring, and a feast. And when the elder son refuses to come in, the father goes out to him too.

This session holds two things together. The first is the grace at the heart of the story, which runs toward people before they have cleaned up and gives no reason to wait passively for a bottom that, with some drugs, can be an overdose. The second is the hard question families carry: how to love someone caught in addiction without making the addiction easier. The study draws on Galatians 6, where Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens and also says that each one should carry his own load. Love helps carry what a person truly cannot carry, and it stops carrying the lies. When a loved one's using turns violent, safety comes first, for the spouse and for the children, before any reconciliation.

keyScripture.why: "But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father runs before the son reaches home or finishes his speech, a picture of grace that does not wait for a person to clean up or prove himself, told to people who resented Jesus for welcoming sinners.

discussion.q: Jesus told this story to people grumbling that he "welcomes sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). Before we read it, who in your life, or in your church, would grumble if Jesus sat down to eat with them?
discussion.behind: Set the context and let it implicate the room. The parable is aimed at religious people who resented the company Jesus kept, not only at the son in the far country. Families sometimes feel that grumbling from church people about their son or daughter, and sometimes they are the ones grumbling. Let both come out. Go first.

discussion.q: Read Luke 15:11-24 aloud. Compare the speech the son rehearses in verses 18-19 with what he actually says in verse 21. What never gets said, and why does it matter?
discussion.behind: Let the room find it: the son never gets to ask to be made like one of the hired servants. The bargaining part of the confession never comes, because the father is already restoring him as a son. Grace does not deny the son's sin, which he confesses, but it refuses his terms for earning his way back. People in recovery often carry a rehearsed speech for God. Let them hear that the father runs before it is finished.

discussion.q: Kenneth Bailey argued that a dignified village father would not run in public, and that this father's run cost him his dignity and took the village's scorn on himself. What does a grace that costs the giver tell you about God, and about what love may cost a family?
discussion.behind: Present Bailey's reading as one scholar's cultural argument rather than something stated in the text; other scholars question it, and the text itself says only that the father ran. Let it deepen the picture without carrying the weight. God's grace is costly to him, which is why it is not cheap, and a family's love will cost something too, without ever requiring anyone to absorb violence.

discussion.q: Paul writes, "Carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2), and three verses later, "each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). Where have you carried a burden someone truly could not carry, and where have you carried a load that was theirs?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge for families. Help the room sort concrete examples. Burdens: rides to treatment, presence, a meal, a call to 911 in an emergency. Loads: lying to employers, paying debts the using created, cleaning up so no one finds out. Don't hand down rules; every family is different and needs counsel. Any situation involving violence calls for safety first and the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

discussion.q: When the elder son refuses to come in, the father goes out and pleads with him too. Who in your family is the elder son, the one who stayed, held everything together, and resents the welcome? What might the father say to them, or to you?
discussion.behind: Close on the elder brother, with self-implication. Siblings, spouses, and parents who held a family together often carry a bitterness they are ashamed of. The father does not dismiss it; he goes out to it. Invite people to name where they stand, the leader first, and leave the parable the way Jesus did, with the elder son's answer unspoken.

objections.objection: If I stop paying for things and covering for him, he could end up on the street or dead. How can letting him face consequences be love?
objections.response: Start with the fear, because it is not an exaggeration. People do die of overdoses, and a parent's or a spouse's terror is love, not weakness. But look at what the rescuing has been doing. Rent money that buys drugs, lies told to the boss, and debts quietly paid usually make the addiction easier to keep, and they rarely bring the person closer to help. There is a third way between rescue and abandonment. Keep saying that you love them and will help them get help. Offer rides to treatment instead of cash. Learn the signs of an overdose and keep naloxone in the house. Get counsel for yourself. You cannot control the outcome, but you can stop paying for the addiction and keep the door to help wide open.

objections.objection: The father in the story let his son go and waited until he came home on his own. Shouldn't I just wait until she hits bottom?
objections.response: Grant what the parable does show. The father does not chase his son into the far country or follow him with money, and there are things a family cannot do for an adult who will not accept help. Letting go of the illusion of control is real wisdom. But the parable is not a technique for handling addiction, and it does not teach families to wait for a bottom. Jesus told it to grumblers about God's welcome, and its point is that the father ran the moment he saw his son. With some drugs, the bottom is an overdose. You can talk with a counselor or a doctor about how to encourage treatment now, you can make it clear that the door to help is open today, and in any medical emergency you call 911. Waiting on God is not the same as waiting for a catastrophe.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you could hear the father in this story say one sentence to you tonight, whether you are the son far off, the elder brother, or the parent watching the road, what would you need it to be?
sessions.practice: This week, if you love someone caught in addiction, write two short lists. On the first, name the burdens you can rightly help carry: a ride to an appointment, a meal, your steady presence, a call to 911 in an emergency. On the second, name the loads that are theirs: the lies you have told for them, the debts their using created, the cleanup that keeps anyone from finding out. Choose one load to set down, and talk with a counselor or a family support group before you do. If anyone in your home is violent or threatening, your first step is safety, not a new boundary: call the National Domestic Violence Hotline (its number is on this site's Find Help page, /help), or 911 in an emergency. If you are the one who has been far off, write the speech you have been rehearsing for God, then read Luke 15:20-24 and notice what never gets said.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you saw us while we were still in the distance, and you ran. We have rehearsed our speeches and bargained for the servant's place, and you have answered with a robe and a ring. Some of us are still far off, some are watching the road for someone we love, and some are standing outside the feast, resentful of the welcome. Meet each of us where we are. Give the families in this room wisdom to love without enabling, and courage to keep themselves and their children safe. Make us a church that runs the way you run. In the name of your Son, who came all the way to the far country for us. Amen.
reflection: Which character in Luke 15 am I most like right now, the son far off, the elder brother, or the parent watching the road, and what do I need from the father?
What burdens can I rightly help carry for someone I love, and what loads have I been carrying that are theirs?
What speech have I been rehearsing to earn my way back to God, and what would it mean to let him answer before I finish it?
sessions.teaching:
Luke sets this story in a particular room. Tax collectors and sinners were gathering to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). Jesus answered with three stories about lost things, a sheep, a coin, and a son, and each ends in a celebration. The third was aimed as much at the grumblers as at anyone in a far country, which matters, because most of us would rather stand in this story as the father than as either son, and it will not let us stay there.

A younger son asks for his share of the estate while his father is still living, leaves for a distant country, and squanders everything in wild living. When famine comes he is feeding pigs and longing to eat what they eat. Then Luke says, "Finally he came to his senses" (Luke 15:17). He rehearses a speech that is honest about his sin and proposes terms he thinks he can live with: he will ask to be made like one of the hired servants and work his way back.

Then the turn: "But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father saw him from far off, as if he had been watching the road, and he doesn't wait for his son to reach the house, finish the speech, or prove he has changed. Kenneth Bailey, who spent forty years teaching the New Testament in the Middle East, argued that a dignified village patriarch would not run in public, and that this father's run was a self-humbling act that took the village's scorn on himself so he could reach his son first. Other scholars doubt how much of that village custom can be read back into the first century, but the text is plain that the father ran. Then look at the speech. In verse 21 the son begins it, but the line about the hired servants never comes, and the father is already calling for the best robe, a ring, sandals, and a feast: "For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!" (Luke 15:24). Grace does not pretend the son didn't squander everything, and the son confesses that he did. What grace refuses is his terms. The story gives no reason to wait passively for a person to hit bottom, and with some drugs the bottom can be an overdose. For anyone in this room who has been far off, the father is not standing at the door with a lecture. He is already on the road.

But families live in the middle of the story, not at the feast, and they carry a hard question: how do you love someone caught in addiction without making the addiction easier? Two instincts compete, and both are love. The first keeps rescuing, paying the rent and making the excuse, because love "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7) and because the alternative might be a funeral; it is right that abandonment can be deadly. The second pulls back hard, cutting off the money and changing the locks, because rescue has only bought more using; it is right that shielding a person from every consequence usually prolongs the addiction. Proverbs observes of a hot-tempered man that "if you rescue him, you will have to do so again" (Proverbs 19:19), and though the proverb is about anger, its wisdom reaches any pattern protected from its own consequences.

Paul gives families a distinction worth learning. "Carry one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), he writes, and three verses later, "For each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). He uses two different words: the burden of verse 2 is a crushing weight no one should bear alone, and the load of verse 5 is the pack each person is responsible to carry. Love helps carry what a person truly cannot carry: a ride to treatment, a meal, steady presence, the call to 911. Enabling carries what is theirs: the lies, the debts their using made, the cleanup that keeps anyone from finding out. Henry Cloud and John Townsend make much of this distinction in their book Boundaries. Love "takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6), and a family that stops lying for the addiction has not stopped loving the person. Families need counsel to hold this line, and they should get it.

Two lines must be drawn without hesitation. First, safety comes before reconciliation. Hitting, threats, breaking things, or controlling where another person goes is abuse, drunk or sober, and no one is required to stay in danger to keep a family together; in immediate danger call 911, and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline to make a safety plan. Second, the children. Jesus was indignant when his disciples kept children away from him, and he took them in his arms (Mark 10:14-16). Children in a home shaped by addiction need safe adults, the truth in words they can understand, and to hear plainly that it is not their fault and not their job to fix. If a child is being harmed or neglected, the child's safety comes first, and church leaders may be required by law to report it.

The story ends outside the house. The elder son, who stayed and worked and, by his own account, never disobeyed, is angry and will not go in, and the father comes out and pleads with him too: "Son, you are always with me ... and all that is mine is yours" (Luke 15:31). Many families have an elder son: the sibling who held things together, the spouse who covered every bill, the parent who is tired of celebrating returns. Their resentment is real, and the father does not dismiss it. He goes out to it. Jesus ends the story without telling us whether the elder son went in, leaving that question to the grumblers, and to us. The father runs down the road for one son and walks out to the field for the other. There is no one in this story he does not go looking for.

scriptureStudy.note: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them." The parable answers a complaint. Jesus tells it to religious people offended by his company, so it is as much about the grumblers as about the son in the far country.

"Finally he came to his senses." The son's turn is real, and his rehearsed speech is honest about his sin. It also proposes terms: he will earn his way back as a hired servant. Many people in recovery carry a speech like it, ready for God.

"He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him." Compassion moves before the confession is spoken. Kenneth Bailey argued that a village patriarch running in public would have shamed himself, which on his reading makes the run a costly act of love.

"Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him" (Luke 15:22). The son begins his speech and never reaches the line about the hired servants. The father restores him as a son before he has proved anything.
"So his father came out and pleaded with him" (Luke 15:28). The father goes out to the resentful son just as he ran to the returning one, and the story ends with the elder son's answer unspoken.

"Carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2), and "each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). Paul uses two different words, a crushing weight that needs many hands and the pack each person must carry. The same passage asks the spiritual to restore a fallen person "with a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1).

"Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (Mark 10:14). Jesus is indignant at those who keep children away. A church that cares for families caught in addiction must see the children, keep them safe, and never make them keepers of the family secret.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long argument about grace that families live inside without naming it. In 1937 Dietrich Bonhoeffer published Nachfolge, known in English as The Cost of Discipleship, and gave the name cheap grace to forgiveness preached without any call to repentance or to follow Christ. A family can practice its own version, a love that has stopped telling the truth, paying for the using and calling it mercy. The opposite failure is love withdrawn until the person earns it back, which looks like strength and is often fear. Luke 15 refuses both. The son confesses his sin, and the father's grace is costly to him rather than cheap, and it still refuses the son's terms for earning his way home.

Weigh the readings of the parable that have shaped the church's imagination. Timothy Keller read it as the story of two lost sons, one lost by breaking the rules and one by keeping them, and pointed out that prodigal means recklessly spendthrift, not wayward, so the word fits the father's grace as well as the younger son. Henri Nouwen, after sitting for hours before Rembrandt's painting of the return, saw himself first in the younger son, then in the elder, and finally heard the call to become the father. A boundary held without grace can harden into a fortress, and grace offered without any boundary can end up paying for the addiction. The discipline is to keep both, with counsel, without confusing a boundary with abandonment or the endurance of abuse with love.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a couple in your group, both in their fifties, say that their twenty-six-year-old son called last week asking for rent money, and that the last three times they sent money for rent it went to drugs. The mother wants to send it anyway, because if he is evicted he will be on the street. The father wants to change the phone number. Both are afraid, and they are angry at each other.

Resist the urge to decide for them. Read Galatians 6:2 and 6:5, and ask the group to help them sort the burden from the load. Someone may suggest paying the landlord directly, or offering a ride to a treatment appointment instead of cash, or telling their son plainly that they love him, will not pay for the using, and will help him get help today. Encourage them to talk with a counselor or a family support group together, and to learn the signs of an overdose and keep naloxone in the house.

Use this to show the room that both parents are loving their son, and that the question is not who loves more but what love should carry. Ask where they have confused rescuing with loving, or pulling back with protecting themselves.

memoryVerse.text: So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.

sessions.title: Something to Live Toward
sessions.aim: To show that freedom in Christ is more than the absence of a substance: a new way of life in community, with the Spirit, a renewed mind, and work and love to give, so that recovery has something to live toward and not only something to run from.
sessions.summary:
Stopping is the first step and a hard one, and many people discover after they stop that the hours the drinking or using once filled are now empty. The loneliness is sharp, and the old friends are dangerous. Families find something similar when a life organized around someone else's addiction begins to change. Jesus told a story about a house swept clean and put in order but left vacant, and what moved back in was worse than before (Matthew 12:43-45). He told it about his own generation, but the warning reaches further. A life emptied of an addiction and left empty does not stay empty.

So the last session asks what freedom is for. Paul writes, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free" (Galatians 5:1), and a few verses later he says what that freedom is for: serving one another in love and walking by the Spirit (Galatians 5:13-16). Romans 12 asks believers to offer their bodies to God and to be renewed in their minds. The letter to the Ephesians describes putting off the old self and putting on the new, and it gets concrete: the thief stops stealing and starts working so that he has something to share (Ephesians 4:28). The pattern is replacement, not only removal, and it happens among people: doctors and counselors, recovery communities, a church that can hear the truth, friends who call, and a place to serve. The study ends without a tidy resolution, because the road is long, but it ends with a direction. Freedom is not an empty house. It is a life with something to live toward.

keyScripture.why: "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). Paul names freedom as Christ's purpose and slavery as a real danger to return to, and in the verses that follow he says what freedom is for: love, service, and walking by the Spirit (Galatians 5:13-16).

discussion.q: If you are in recovery, what filled the hours that drinking or using used to fill? If you love someone who is caught, what has your own life been organized around, and what is left when that begins to change?
