discussion.behind: Open with the empty house, concretely. People in early recovery often find the hours after stopping lonely and dangerous, and families often find that their own lives shrank around the crisis. Let both name what is empty, and don't rush to fill it with answers.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 12:43-45. Jesus told this about his own generation. What does the picture of a house swept clean but left vacant warn us about a recovery that only removes?
discussion.behind: Be honest about the context: Jesus is warning a generation that had seen his works and still would not receive him. The principle the study draws is careful and limited: a life emptied of an addiction and left empty is vulnerable. Don't turn this into a frightening story about relapse or about spirits. Use it to ask what fills the house.

discussion.q: Paul writes, "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13). Why does he tie freedom to serving other people, and what might serving look like for someone in recovery?
discussion.behind: Freedom in Galatians is release for love, not the absence of all restraint. Service gives a person in recovery a place in the community, a reason to get up, and the dignity of being needed. Don't push anyone in early recovery into a role they are not ready for. Small service counts.

discussion.q: The letter to the Ephesians tells the thief to stop stealing and start working, "that he may have something to share with the one in need" (Ephesians 4:28). What new thing could you put on in place of the thing you, or your family, are trying to put off?
discussion.behind: Make the replacement concrete: lies replaced by truth-telling; the old evening ritual by a phone call, a meeting, or a meal with someone; the hours of covering for someone by a life of one's own. Putting off and putting on belong together. Let families answer too, because their old pattern may be control or constant vigilance.

discussion.q: As this study ends, who are the people you will walk with from here, and where is one place you can belong, whether a recovery community, a church, or a friendship, where the truth can be told?
discussion.behind: Close the study with community rather than a resolution, and make sure every person leaves with at least one name and one place. Name, without endorsing any particular program, that recovery communities and church recovery ministries exist, and that the church should be a place where people in recovery belong. Leader, go first, and say where you yourself will go for honesty.

objections.objection: I don't need a whole new life. I just need to stop drinking. All this talk about purpose and community makes it sound more complicated than it is.
objections.response: Grant the urgency. Stopping comes first, and for someone whose body depends on a substance, stopping safely with a doctor is the most important thing this week; no one should wait for a new life before getting help. But many people discover after they stop that the hours are empty and the loneliness can pull harder than the craving did. Jesus' story of the swept house left vacant names the risk, and Scripture's pattern is replacement as well as removal. The letter to the Ephesians doesn't only tell the thief to stop stealing; it tells him to work so that he can give (Ephesians 4:28). And it tells the drinker, "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18).

objections.objection: I'm not a church person. My recovery group has helped me more than any church ever did. Why would I trade that for this?
objections.response: No one is asking you to trade anything that is keeping you alive. Many people have found in recovery communities a daily honesty and company they never found in a church, and where churches have been places of performance or contempt, the church should confess it rather than defend itself. Keep going to what helps. This study asks a different question: where does the freedom finally come from, and what is it for? Paul's answer is a person, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free" (Galatians 5:1), and a people who "serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13). If a church has not been that for you, the failure belongs to the church. The invitation still stands, and some churches are learning to be places where a person in recovery is welcome to tell the truth.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you imagine yourself a year from now, free in the way Galatians 5 describes, what would you be doing with the hours, and with whom?
sessions.practice: This week, write a simple rule for the next seven days with four lines: one thing to put off, one thing to put on in its place, one person to call each day, and one small way to serve someone else. Keep it small enough to keep. If you drink or use every day and have not yet talked to a doctor, that call is the first line. If you love someone in recovery, write a rule for your own life too, one not organized around managing theirs. The rule of life builder on this site, /tools/rule-of-life, can help you shape it. Pray Galatians 5:1 each morning, and at the end of the week tell one person what you put on.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you set us free for freedom, and you did not free us to live in an empty house. Fill the hours the addiction once filled with your Spirit, with friendship, with honest work, and with ways to serve. Give the people in this room a community where the truth can be told and a place where they are needed, and give the families a life of their own again. The road is long, but we are not walking it alone. Keep us from returning to the yoke of slavery, and when we stumble, lift us again. We wait for the day you redeem our bodies and set the whole creation free. Until then, keep us walking with you and with each other. Amen.
reflection: What hours, habits, or relationships have been left empty by what I am putting off, and what is beginning to fill them?
What is one thing I could put on, in the pattern of Ephesians 4, in place of the thing I am putting off?
Who will I walk with from here, and where can I belong as someone who tells the truth?
sessions.teaching:
Stopping is the first step and one of the hardest, and for someone whose body depends on alcohol or another drug, stopping safely with a doctor's help is the most urgent thing there is. But many people discover after they stop that the hours the drinking or using once filled are now empty. The evenings are long, the old friends are dangerous, and the loneliness can pull harder than the craving did. Families find something similar when a life organized around someone else's addiction begins to change. So the last session asks what freedom is for.

Jesus told a short, unsettling story about an unclean spirit that leaves a man, wanders, and comes back to find "the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order" (Matthew 12:44). It moves back in with seven others, "and the final plight of that man is worse than the first" (Matthew 12:45). Jesus told it as a warning to his own generation, which had seen his works and still would not receive him, and we should not turn it into a ghost story about relapse. But the principle reaches further than its first hearers. A house emptied and left empty does not stay empty.

Paul's letter to the Galatians puts freedom at the center. He was writing to churches tempted to add circumcision and the law of Moses to faith in Christ, not to people in recovery, but he knew that freedom can be lost: "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). Then he says what freedom is for: "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13), and "walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). Notice the order. Paul doesn't say to defeat the desires first and then walk with God. He says to walk by the Spirit, and the desires lose their rule. Freedom is release from a cruel master for a life of love.

Romans 12 makes the same move with the body: "Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God" (Romans 12:1). Addiction is lived in the body, and the body once handed over to a substance is invited to be offered to God, out of mercy rather than fear. Then comes the mind: "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2), a process rather than an event. The letter to the Ephesians describes the same change as putting off and putting on: "to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:22-24). Then it gets practical, and its commands come in two halves. The thief "must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need" (Ephesians 4:28), so the man who took becomes a man who gives. And in the next chapter: "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18).

Augustine came to faith in a garden in Milan in 386 after reading words from Romans 13: "Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh" (Romans 13:14). Two practical truths sit in that verse. The first is to clothe yourself with Christ, a new allegiance and a greater love. Augustine's word for the human problem was disordered love, loving lesser things as though they were God, and his hope was not a stronger will but love set in order by grace. The second is to make no provision, which in recovery is plain wisdom: once a doctor has helped you plan to stop safely, get it out of the house, change the route home, delete the number, and stay away from the places where the old life waits.

None of this happens alone. "Two are better than one," the Teacher says in Ecclesiastes, and "if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Recovery happens among people: doctors and counselors, treatment programs, recovery communities, and a church that can hear the truth about a relapse without gossip or panic. Recovery groups and church recovery ministries meet in many places, and many people have found in them an honesty the church preaches more often than it practices. The church should not compete with them but become a community where a person in recovery is welcome to tell the truth, to be known by name rather than by their worst years, and to serve. Paul told the Corinthians, after a list that includes drunkards, "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11). Faithful Christians differ about whether a person in recovery should keep naming himself by what he is recovering from, and this study leaves that open. Both sides guard something true: the honesty that knows it can fall, and the new identity God gives.

The study ends without a tidy resolution, because the road back is long and some in this room are still on its first mile. Some are still using. Some are waiting for someone who is. Paul knew that freedom in this life is real and also partial. He wrote that the whole creation is waiting to "be set free from its bondage to decay" (Romans 8:21), and that we ourselves "groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). The body that craved will one day be redeemed. Until then, freedom is kept the way Paul says it is kept, by standing firm and walking by the Spirit, among people who know the truth about us.

scriptureStudy.note: "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free." Freedom is not a reward for staying sober; it is what Christ has done. The command that follows assumes slavery is a real danger: "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery."

"Rather, serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13). Freedom is release for love, and Paul sums up the law in loving your neighbor as yourself. The flesh loses its rule as believers walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16), not as they grit their teeth alone.

"Be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2). The body once handed over to a substance is offered to God "on account of God's mercy" (Romans 12:1), and the mind is renewed over time, which is what the slow rebuilding of thought and habit in recovery looks like.

"To put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires" (Ephesians 4:22). Anyone who has believed the lie of just one more knows what deceitful desires are. The new self is put on, created to be like God.

"He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need." The letter does not end with the prohibition. The thief becomes a worker and then a giver.

"Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). The alternative to drunkenness is fullness, and the verses that follow are communal: psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs spoken to one another, and thanksgiving.

"Pity the one who falls without another to help him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The Teacher states plainly what recovery teaches: people fall, and the one who falls alone is in danger. "A cord of three strands is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12).

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the question of what fills the house, because the church's oldest answers to vice were not only about stopping. Augustine named the human problem disordered love, loving lesser goods as though they were God, and his remedy was love set in order by grace. Gerald May and Edward Welch, met in the first session, come at the same ground from different sides, May through desire and Welch through worship, and both insist that the remedy has to reach the heart and not only the habit. Eugene Peterson's meditations on the Songs of Ascents picture discipleship as pilgrims going up together to worship.

A serious group should weigh these voices with honesty about the church's record. Recovery communities have often practiced the confession, mutual help, and daily dependence the New Testament describes, while churches have sometimes offered a Sunday performance and a weekday silence. The discipline is not to replace treatment or recovery communities but to become a church where a person in recovery can belong, serve, and be known, remembering that the final hope is not a well-managed habit but the redemption of our bodies and the freedom of the children of God.
sessions.caseStudy:
Imagine a woman in your group who has been sober for nearly a year. She came to the first session terrified and is now steady, and she tells the group that the hardest part right now is not craving but emptiness. Her evenings used to be organized around drinking. Now they are long and quiet, her old friends still drink, and she has started to wonder whether this is all there is.

The room may want to congratulate her and move on. Don't. Read Matthew 12:44 and Ephesians 4:28, and ask the group what could move into the house. Someone may know a ministry that needs a reliable volunteer on weeknights, or a household that would welcome her for dinner, or a person in recovery who would be glad of a regular phone call. Encourage her to keep going to whatever recovery community has been helping her.

Use this to show the room that recovery is more than removal, and that the church's part is to make room. Ask what would fill their own house, and whose house they could help to fill.

memoryVerse.text: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.

leaderPrimer:
Your room may hold all of these at once: someone still drinking or using who came because a spouse insisted, someone with years of recovery who knows more about this than you do, someone a few weeks sober and shaking, a mother who has not slept through the night since her son started using, an adult who grew up in a house where the bottle set the weather, someone grieving a person who died of an overdose. They need different things from you, and they have one thing in common: each has been lectured, and each can sense a lecture coming. The hazard of leading this study is the urge to fix, to tell the person still using what he ought to do, to tell the mother what she should have done, to hand the newly sober a verse as though it were a treatment plan. Resist it. Keep the room safe and honest, keep pointing at the text, and don't be shocked by anything.

Say plainly, at the first meeting and whenever it matters again, that this study is a companion to treatment and to recovery communities, never a substitute for them. Recovery groups and church recovery ministries meet in many communities, and many people find in them a daily honesty and company that a five-session study cannot give; encourage people to keep going to whatever is keeping them alive. Know where help is before anyone asks. SAMHSA's National Helpline is free and confidential, answers at any hour in English and Spanish, and refers people to treatment, though it is not crisis counseling; 988 also answers for a substance use crisis, and for anyone worried about someone else. Before the first session, copy the numbers you may need from the site's Find Help page, /help, where they are kept current, and keep them with you. The care page on this site, /help/addiction, gathers the first steps, and the eight-week plan at /plans/addiction can carry a person between sessions. You are not a counselor or a physician, and nothing in this guide is medical or legal advice.

Every leader must know two medical facts. First, stopping alcohol, and some other drugs, including some prescription sedatives, suddenly can be dangerous, even life-threatening. Anyone who drinks or uses every day should not quit alone but with a doctor's help, and you should say so before anyone in your group resolves to quit cold tonight. A doctor can help a person stop safely, at home or in a hospital or detox program. If someone has a seizure, a fever, severe confusion, or hallucinations after cutting back or stopping, call 911. Second, an overdose is a 911 emergency. If someone cannot be woken, is breathing very slowly or not at all, or has blue lips or fingertips, call 911, give naloxone if it is on hand (it is now sold without a prescription), lay the person on their side, and stay with them until help arrives, even if they wake, because naloxone can wear off before the drug does. After a stretch of not using, tolerance drops, and returning to the old amount of an opioid can kill, so a relapse is never only a spiritual matter. Some in your room may be taking a medication their doctor prescribed for alcohol or opioid use disorder. That is medical treatment; never let anyone be shamed for it.

If someone is using in a way that endangers themselves or others, stop and act. If a person arrives impaired, don't let them drive; arrange a ride, and call 911 if anyone is in immediate danger. Talk with the person privately, never in front of the group. If anyone speaks of not wanting to live, of suicide, or of everyone being better off without them, take it seriously every time. Don't move on to the next question. Speak with them privately, stay with them, and call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, together; in immediate danger, call 911.

If someone's drinking or using at home has turned violent or threatening, safety comes first, before reconciliation and before any confrontation. Never counsel anyone to stay in danger to keep a family together, and never urge anyone to confront a violent person. Point them to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, which helps people make a safety plan at any hour by phone, text, or online chat, and to 911 in immediate danger. If a child is being harmed or neglected, the child's safety comes first. Church leaders may be mandated reporters of child abuse and neglect, the laws vary by state, and you must know your own obligations before the study begins; your church's leadership can help you find out. Never ask anyone to disclose danger, abuse, or thoughts of suicide in the group. When it comes out anyway, stop, thank them, talk privately as soon as you can, and connect them to help.

Set the rule of confidentiality at the first meeting and keep it: what is said in the room stays in the room. State its limits just as plainly. If someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or a child is being harmed, you will not keep that secret, and you may be required by law to report it. Never promise more secrecy than you can keep. Think about who is in the room together. A husband who drinks and the wife who has been covering for him may not be able to speak honestly in the same group, and where there has been violence they should not be placed in one. Talk with people before the study begins when you can.

Some questions this study raises are open among faithful Christians, and the guide leaves them open; it does not say where James Bell lands on any of them. The first is whom Paul describes in Romans 7:14-25. Those who hear the believer's ongoing struggle point to the present tense and to a man who delights in God's law in his inner being (Romans 7:22), as only a renewed heart can; Augustine came to this view later in life, and Luther and Calvin followed him. Those who hear life under the law, before or apart from Christ, point to a man "sold as a slave to sin" (Romans 7:14) when the chapter before says believers have been set free from sin, and to the absence of the Spirit from these verses when chapter 8 speaks of him again and again; many early Greek interpreters read it this way, as do many modern scholars. The others are whether a Christian may drink in moderation or should abstain, whether addiction is best called a disease, a sin, a habit, or something that needs more than one of those words, and whether a person in recovery should keep naming himself by what he is recovering from. The first session and the questions at the back of this guide give the strongest case on each side. State each position so that its own defenders would recognize it, let people disagree and remain brothers and sisters, and don't let the group become a debate about them. Your church's pastors and your own tradition will have more to say.

You don't need to have been where they are. You do need to be honest about where you have been. A leader who seems never to have needed anything to get through a day will probably lose the room by the second session; a leader who admits the divided will, without pretending a small habit is the same as a body's dependence, can keep it. The study ends at Galatians 5, with freedom and a life to live toward, and many in your room will arrive there still struggling, some still using. Let them. Five sessions will not end anyone's addiction. They can begin to end the hiding and the loneliness, and they can answer the lie that God is finished with them. Keep the door open, and keep pointing to the Father who runs.

faq.q: Does this study say addiction is a sin or a disease?
faq.a: It refuses to make you choose one word and throw the other away. It takes the medical account at its strongest, that repeated use changes the brain's circuits for reward, stress, and self-control, and the moral account at its strongest, that Scripture names drunkenness as sin and recovery asks a person to own their choices. Then it reads Romans 7, where Paul sees another law at work in his body, "holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me" (Romans 7:23), and is responsible and captive at once. Faithful Christians differ about the best vocabulary, and the study leaves it open while refusing both contempt and excuse.

faq.q: I drink or use every day. Should I just stop right now?
faq.a: Please don't stop suddenly on your own. Stopping alcohol, and some other drugs, including some prescription sedatives, can be dangerous, even life-threatening. Talk to a doctor first, or call SAMHSA's National Helpline (its number is on this site's Find Help page, /help), and stop with medical help. That isn't a lack of faith; it's the honesty the first session is about. A doctor can help you stop safely, at home or in a hospital or detox program, and if your pills were prescribed, talk with the prescriber before changing the dose. If a seizure, a fever, severe confusion, or hallucinations follow cutting back or stopping, call 911. If you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988 now. This guide is not medical advice; it is meant to get you to the people who can give it.

faq.q: What should we do if someone overdoses?
faq.a: Call 911. An overdose is a medical emergency, never something for a group to handle on its own. If someone cannot be woken, is breathing very slowly or not at all, or has blue lips or fingertips, call 911, give naloxone if you have it, lay the person on their side so they don't choke, and stay with them until help arrives, even if they wake, because naloxone can wear off before the drug does. Naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose, and in 2023 a nasal spray form was approved for sale without a prescription, so families and churches can keep it on hand. After a stretch without using, tolerance drops, so a relapse can be more dangerous than the old habit was. This is basic safety information, not medical advice.

faq.q: Is it a sin for a Christian to drink at all?
faq.a: Faithful Christians disagree, and this study does not settle it. Some hold that Scripture permits wine in moderation, pointing to the wine that gladdens the heart in Psalm 104:15, to Jesus turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana (John 2), and to Scripture's condemnation of drunkenness rather than of drink (Ephesians 5:18); to forbid what God has given, they say, is to add a rule Scripture does not make. Others hold that abstaining is the wiser and more loving course, pointing to Scripture's sober warnings about wine (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29-35), to the harm alcohol does to bodies and families, and to Paul's counsel that it is better not to drink wine or do anything that causes a brother to stumble (Romans 14:21); love, they say, gladly gives up a freedom for the sake of someone who could fall. Both agree that drunkenness is sin, and both would say that a person whose drinking has mastered them faces a different question from a person who has a glass at dinner. For that person, both sides would counsel the same first step: get help, starting with a doctor.

faq.q: I relapsed. Does that mean my faith, or my recovery, was fake?
faq.a: No, and the third session was written for you. Scripture's saints fell after their vows, Peter within hours of his, and the Lord who restored him did not treat the fall as proof that Peter had never loved him. Medicine says something similar: the National Institute on Drug Abuse compares relapse to the return of symptoms in other chronic illnesses, a sign that treatment needs to be resumed or changed, not proof that it failed. None of that makes a relapse small. Tell someone today and call your doctor or counselor. If you use opioids, be especially careful, because after time away your tolerance is lower and the old amount can kill. Then come back to the room. The door has not closed.

faq.q: Do I have to tell the group what I have done?
faq.a: No. No one is ever required to disclose anything in this group, and leaders are told never to ask for it. The letter of James tells believers to confess their sins to each other, and the second session takes that seriously, but confession is usually wisest with one or two people you trust, such as a pastor, a counselor, or a mature friend, rather than a whole room. What the group asks is honesty at whatever depth you can bear and a promise to keep what others say in the room. Your leader will explain the limits of that promise: when someone is in danger, or a child is being harmed, it cannot be kept.

faq.q: My spouse drinks and becomes violent. What does this study say to me?
faq.a: That your safety comes first: before reconciliation, before any confrontation, and before keeping the family together. Hitting, threats, breaking things, and controlling where you go or whom you see are abuse, whether the person is drunk or sober, and they are not a drinking problem for you to manage with more patience. Nothing in Scripture asks you to stay in danger. If you are in immediate danger, call 911. The National Domestic Violence Hotline can help you make a safety plan at any hour, by phone, text, or online chat; its numbers are on this site's Find Help page, /help, and in the help box printed with this guide. If someone checks your phone or computer, look for help on a device they cannot see. Their using is not your fault, and their violence is not the price of your love.

faq.q: How do I love my adult child, or my spouse, without enabling the addiction?
faq.a: The fourth session works on exactly this. It draws on a distinction Paul makes in Galatians 6 between the heavy burdens we carry for one another and the load each person must carry himself. Love helps carry what a person truly cannot carry: a ride to treatment, a call to the doctor, a meal, a steady presence. Enabling carries what is theirs to carry: the lies told on their behalf, the bills their using created, the consequences it should have brought. The study also refuses the opposite error, love withdrawn until they hit bottom, because with some drugs the bottom can be an overdose. Families need their own help here, from a counselor or a family support group, and their own safety comes first.

Children in a home shaped by addiction need safe adults, the truth in words they can understand, and to hear plainly that the drinking or using is not their fault and not their job to fix. Jesus was indignant when his disciples kept children away from him, and the church should be the last place a child is told to keep the family secret. If a child is being harmed or neglected, the child's safety comes first. Church leaders may be mandated reporters, the laws vary by state, and leaders should know their obligations before the study begins. A parent in recovery can ask their children's forgiveness and repair what can be repaired, in ways that suit their age, ideally with a counselor's help.

faq.q: Is taking a medication for addiction just trading one drug for another?
faq.a: This study will not ask you to make medical decisions, and it will not let anyone in the room be shamed for following a doctor's treatment. The Food and Drug Administration has approved medications for alcohol use disorder and for opioid use disorder, used together with counseling and other care, and for many people they are part of treatment. Whether a medication is right for you, and for how long, is a question for your doctor. What Christians can say is that God's care reaches people through medicine as truly as through prayer, and that a person taking a prescribed medication while working at recovery is receiving care, not cheating.

faq.q: Once an addict, always an addict?
faq.a: If the phrase means that a person can never change, or can never be trusted again, it is not a sentence any Christian should pass on anyone. Paul told the Corinthians, after naming drunkards among others, "And that is what some of you were" (1 Corinthians 6:11). But underneath the slogan sits a real question that faithful Christians answer differently, and the study leaves it open: whether a person in recovery should keep naming himself by what he is recovering from. Many do, and they have good reasons. It keeps them honest, it guards against the pride that says I'm past this, and it echoes Paul's warning that "the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12); the first letter to Timothy even has Paul call himself the worst of sinners, in the present tense (1 Timothy 1:15). Others ask whether a believer's deepest name should be the thing Christ has washed, and they hear in Paul's past tense, what some of you were, a new name already given. Each side protects something true, honesty about ongoing vulnerability and the identity God gives, and the fifth session lets the room weigh both.

faq.q: I'm not religious. Isn't this just the church telling addicted people to pray harder?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and churches have earned it. This study refuses the version you are worried about. It says plainly that prayer is no substitute for a doctor, that stopping some substances without medical help is dangerous, and that shame is no cure for addiction. It takes the medical account of addiction seriously. What it adds is a claim you can weigh: that the divided will Paul describes, wanting the good and doing what you hate, is a true description of human beings and not only of people caught in addiction, and that the way out is not a technique but a person who receives people before they have cleaned up. You don't have to believe that to find the study honest. It asks only that you weigh it.

faq.q: Can I lead this if I am in recovery myself, or if addiction has wounded my family?
faq.a: Yes, and you may lead it better than someone who has never been near it. But guard your own recovery first. Don't lead alone; ask a co-leader to share the room and the follow-up, keep your own support in place outside the group, and don't let the group become the place where you work through your own story. You never have to disclose your history in order to lead, and you should not tell more than you would want repeated. If a session stirs up something you can't carry, tell your co-leader, your pastor, or your counselor, and take care of it.

timeline.event: Jerusalem falls to Babylon. In the poems of Lamentations, written in the aftermath, the poet remembers his affliction and wandering and, in the middle of the ruin, calls to mind that the mercies of the LORD are new every morning (Lamentations 3:19-23).

Criticized for welcoming sinners and eating with them, Jesus answers with three stories of lost things, the last about a father who runs to a son still far off and then goes out to plead with the elder brother who will not come in (Luke 15).

Paul writes to the church in Rome, most likely from Corinth, describing a self that does what it hates and cries out for a rescuer, and then declaring that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 7:15-8:1).

Augustine, thirty-one years old, after years of asking God for chastity but not yet, reads Paul's words in Romans 13:13-14 in a garden in Milan and comes to faith. Ambrose baptizes him at Easter the following year.

Augustine writes the Confessions. The eighth book traces how lust indulged became habit and habit became a necessity he could not break, reaching for Romans 7 to describe it; the tenth examines the temptations that remained years after his conversion.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer publishes Nachfolge, known in English as The Cost of Discipleship, in Nazi Germany, and gives the name cheap grace to forgiveness preached without any call to repentance or to follow Christ.

Bonhoeffer writes Life Together in Göttingen in 1938, and it is published in 1939. Its last chapter, on confession and communion, argues that sin isolates and that confession to a brother or sister breaks through into community.
By the account of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the first wave of the opioid overdose epidemic begins with increased prescribing of opioids.
The Food and Drug Administration approves a naloxone nasal spray for sale without a prescription, putting a medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose within reach of families and churches.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for coming, and thank you for the courage it took, because addiction is one of the hardest things to talk about honestly in a church. Before we start, a few things. First, what is said in this room stays in this room, with one exception: if someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or a child is being harmed, I will not keep that secret, and I may be required to get help. Second, no one here has to share anything; you are welcome to listen the whole time. Third, this group is not treatment. It walks alongside doctors, counselors, treatment programs, and recovery groups, and it never replaces them. If you drink or use every day, please don't stop suddenly on your own, because that can be dangerous; the right first step is a doctor. If anyone here ever overdoses, we call 911. Fourth, none of us stands above this. Some here may have been caught, some may love someone who is, and all of us know what it is to want the good and fail to do it. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we will sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the hours where this is actually fought, the drive home past the store, the phone that rings at midnight, the morning after, because that is where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though nothing is finished, because recovery is never finished in an evening and pretending otherwise would be a lie. If something tonight told you that you need help, a doctor, a counselor, a treatment program, or a recovery group, please hear that as God's kindness and not as failure, and talk with me afterward if you want help finding it. If you are in danger, or thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency, and tell me. Try the practice if you can. And remember that what was said here stays here, with the one exception I named at the start. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules on confidentiality and its limits, say that the group walks alongside treatment and never replaces it, and name the two safety facts: no stopping daily drinking or using without a doctor, and an overdose is a 911 emergency.
Week 2: Session 1, I Do What I Hate, with extended time on Romans 7:15-25.
Week 3: Session 2, Out of Hiding, with time for families to name the secrets they have kept.
Week 4: Session 3, The Pit and the Waiting, including each person's plan for the hardest hour.
Week 5: Session 4, The Father Running, part one: the parable and a grace that does not wait for a bottom.
Week 6: Session 4, part two: love without enabling, safety first, and care for the children. Consider meeting with family members separately this week.
Week 7: Session 5, Something to Live Toward, with each person's simple rule for the week.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the practices and memory verses, and make sure every person leaves with one name to call, one place to belong, and, if they need it, a next step toward treatment.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, with the ground rules and safety facts set at the start. Plan a longer meeting, or use three discussion questions from each session.
Week 2: Session 3, The Pit and the Waiting, with extended time on what to do after a relapse.
Week 3: Session 4, The Father Running, with extended time on love without enabling and on safety.
Week 4: Session 5, Something to Live Toward, closing with each person naming one person to call and one place to belong.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, I Do What I Hate.
Week 3: Session 3, The Pit and the Waiting.
Week 5: Session 5, Something to Live Toward.

bibliography.title: Addiction and Grace
bibliography.author: Gerald G. May
bibliography.note: A psychiatrist and spiritual counselor who worked with chemically dependent patients argues that addiction is a process of attachment at work in every human heart, binding a longing meant for love and for God to things that cannot satisfy it, and that freedom comes by grace rather than by willpower or self-management. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave: Finding Hope in the Power of the Gospel
bibliography.author: Edward T. Welch
bibliography.note: A psychologist and counselor at the Christian Counseling and Educational Foundation reads addiction as a problem of the heart and of worship, in which we serve ourselves and our desires instead of the true God, and presses that diagnosis toward the hope of the gospel. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Addiction and Virtue: Beyond the Models of Disease and Choice
bibliography.author: Kent Dunnington
bibliography.note: A philosopher argues that neither the disease model nor the choice model accounts for what people in addiction experience, and draws on Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas to describe addiction in terms of habit, which mediates between the two. The spine of session 1's steelman.

bibliography.title: Alcohol, Addiction and Christian Ethics
bibliography.author: Christopher C. H. Cook
bibliography.note: Explores how the divided self in Paul and the divided will in Augustine can inform and extend scientific accounts of addictive disorder, which is marked by a will divided between the desire to continue and the desire to stop. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written about 397 to 400. The eighth book traces will becoming lust, lust becoming habit, and habit becoming necessity, and tells of the conversion in a Milan garden in 386; the tenth examines the temptations that remained. Sessions 1, 3, and 5.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written in 1938 and published in 1939. Its final chapter, on confession and communion, argues that sin isolates the sinner and that confession to a brother or sister breaks through into community. The theological spine of session 2.

bibliography.title: Dopamine Nation: Finding Balance in the Age of Indulgence
bibliography.author: Anna Lembke
bibliography.note: A Stanford addiction psychiatrist describes the brain's balance between pleasure and pain, explains why constant reward leaves people needing more to feel pleasure, and commends abstinence, radical honesty, and what she calls prosocial shame, shame met by a community with accountability and support rather than exile. A secular source tested against Scripture in session 2.

bibliography.title: Finding the Lost: Cultural Keys to Luke 15
bibliography.author: Kenneth E. Bailey
bibliography.note: A scholar who spent forty years teaching the New Testament in the Middle East reads the three parables of Luke 15 against village culture, arguing that a dignified father would not run in public and that this father's run takes the village's scorn on himself to protect his son. Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: The Prodigal God: Recovering the Heart of the Christian Faith
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Reads Luke 15 as the story of two lost sons, one lost by breaking the rules and one by keeping them, and points out that prodigal means recklessly spendthrift, not wayward, so the word fits the father's grace as well as the younger son. Supports session 4's attention to the elder brother.

bibliography.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
bibliography.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen
bibliography.note: A meditation on Rembrandt's painting of the parable, which Nouwen sat with for hours at the Hermitage, in which he recognizes himself in the younger son, then in the resentful elder son, and finally hears the call to become the welcoming father. Supports session 4.

bibliography.title: Boundaries
bibliography.author: Henry Cloud and John Townsend
bibliography.note: A widely read Christian book on being responsible to others and for ourselves, which makes much of the distinction between the burdens we carry for one another and the load each person carries in Galatians 6:2 and 6:5. Useful for families in session 4, read with a counselor wherever there is danger.

bibliography.title: A Long Obedience in the Same Direction: Discipleship in an Instant Society
bibliography.author: Eugene H. Peterson
bibliography.note: Meditations on the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, offered as a guide to persevering discipleship in a culture that wants instant results. Supports sessions 3 and 5.

furtherReading: Addiction and Grace, Gerald G. May, for readers who want to see addiction as a captivity of desire that touches every human heart, and freedom as a gift of grace rather than a feat of willpower.
Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave, Edward T. Welch, for those who want a biblical counselor's account of addiction as a matter of the heart and of worship, pressed toward the hope of the gospel.
Boundaries, Henry Cloud and John Townsend, for families learning the difference between helping carry a burden and carrying someone else's load, read with a counselor wherever there is danger.
The Return of the Prodigal Son, Henri J. M. Nouwen, for anyone who has been the younger son, the elder son, or the parent watching the road.
A Long Obedience in the Same Direction, Eugene H. Peterson, for people in recovery and the families waiting with them who need a picture of faithfulness measured in years rather than days.

glossary.definition: A pattern of compulsive use of a substance or behavior that continues despite harm, in which wanting to stop and being able to stop have come apart. The study describes addiction without diagnosing anyone; only a qualified professional can assess a person's condition.

Scripture's picture of a will held captive, as in Romans 7 and John 8, where a person both chooses and is mastered, wanting the good and doing what he hates. Christopher Cook has argued that this divided will sheds light on addictive disorder. The study uses the word alongside medical language, not instead of it.

In the tradition of Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas, a settled disposition formed by repeated action, a second nature. Kent Dunnington uses the idea to stand between the disease and choice models of addiction.

An intense desire for a substance or behavior, often set off by stress, places, people, or times of day. The letter to the Ephesians describes a life given over to impurity "with a craving for more" (Ephesians 4:19).

The physical and mental symptoms that can follow when a body that depends on a substance goes without it. Withdrawal from alcohol and some other drugs, including some prescription sedatives, can be dangerous, which is why stopping should be done with a doctor.

Taking more of a substance than the body can survive without help. It is a 911 emergency. Signs of an opioid overdose include being unable to wake, very slow or stopped breathing, and blue lips or fingertips.
A medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose. In 2023 a nasal spray form was approved for sale without a prescription. It never replaces a call to 911.

A return to drinking or using after a period without. The study treats it as an occasion to get help at once, neither the end of hope nor a small thing, and warns that after time away tolerance is lower, so the old amount of an opioid can be fatal.

The long work of living free of a substance or behavior that once ruled, usually with medical care, counseling, and the company of others. The study calls it a long obedience, measured in years and not meant to be carried alone.

Shielding a person from the consequences of their drinking or using, by lying for them, paying for what their using cost, or cleaning up after it, so that the addiction becomes easier to keep. From inside a family, love and enabling can look alike.

A clear limit on what a person will do or allow, held for the sake of truth and safety rather than punishment. Galatians 6 distinguishes the burdens we carry for one another from the load each person must carry himself.

Telling the truth about sin to God and, as the letter of James says, to one another, so that what was hidden loses its power. It is wisest with one or two trusted people, never forced, and never a public spectacle.

The sense of being not only guilty of something but defective, which drives a person into hiding, as in the garden of Genesis 3. Shame met with contempt often drives people deeper into addiction; shame brought into the light and met with grace can begin to heal.
Bonhoeffer's name for forgiveness preached without any call to repentance or to follow Christ. The study sees a family version of it in enabling, love that has stopped telling the truth.
In Galatians 5, not the absence of all restraint but release from slavery for a life of love, service, and walking by the Spirit.
The pattern of change in Ephesians 4:22-24, in which an old way of life is set aside and a new self, created to be like God, is put on. Stopping is joined to starting.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Churches have often met addiction in one of two wrong ways, with contempt that drives people into hiding or with a silence that leaves families alone. It is for people who can't stop, people in recovery, and the families who love them. It walks alongside treatment and recovery groups and never replaces them. Come honest, not finished.

promoKit.inviteCaption: Paul wrote, "But what I hate, I do" (Romans 7:15). A five-session study on addiction, recovery, and the God who runs toward people still far off, for those who are caught and the families who love them. Not a treatment program, and not a lecture. Come honest, not finished.
quoteCards: You can be responsible for what you do and held captive by it at the same time. Paul describes exactly that in Romans 7.
Shame is no cure for addiction. Mostly it teaches people where to hide.
The first question God asks in Scripture is, "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). It wasn't a request for information. It was an invitation out of hiding.
A relapse is not the end of the story, and it is not nothing. It is the moment to call for help.
The father did not wait for the speech. He ran while his son was still in the distance.
Love helps carry the burdens a person cannot carry. It stops carrying the lies.
Freedom in Christ is not an empty house. It is a life with something to live toward.
A church where no one can say I relapsed is a church where people stay hidden until it is too late.
